name: AI Fairness / Machine Learning
core_concern: Whether group-level fairness metrics are reliable when base rates differ across subgroups — Simpson's Paradox as a structural threat to audit validity
primary_venue: FAccT; NeurIPS; Big Data journal; VLDB
key_claim: Chouldechova (2017) impossibility theorem: calibration and equal error rates are simultaneously unachievable when prevalence differs across groups. Differing base rates ARE the paradox mechanism in disguise.
open_question: Whether the FAccT community explicitly frames its impossibility results as Simpson's Paradox instances or treats base-rate divergence as a distinct phenomenon

name: Bayesian / Decision-Theoretic
core_concern: Whether Bayesian model-selection criteria (Bayes factors, posterior predictive) are themselves susceptible to Simpson-type reversals
primary_venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B; Bayesian Analysis
key_claim: Lindley (1997): Bayes factor proponents can simultaneously conclude tall men > tall women AND short men > short women AND women > men overall — a Simpson reversal in posterior odds. The paradox lives inside Bayesian inference, not just frequentist aggregation.
open_question: Whether prior specification can fully neutralise the reversal or whether the paradox is structurally unavoidable in hierarchical Bayesian models

name: Causal Graphical / DAG Tradition
core_concern: Identifying the structural (graph) conditions under which stratification resolves or worsens the paradox
primary_venue: JMLR; UAI; Artificial Intelligence; MIT Press books
key_claim: The paradox is a confounding problem solvable via the back-door criterion; a DAG over observed variables determines which table (pooled or stratified) is the correct one
open_question: Dong, Cai & Zhao (2024): confounding is not the universal source — inter-unit causation and accidental associations also produce the paradox, so DAG adjustment alone is insufficient

name: Epidemiology / Observational Studies
core_concern: Noncollapsibility: when does controlling for a confounder change the measure of association, and when is that change meaningful?
primary_venue: Epidemiology; American Journal of Epidemiology; Statistical Science
key_claim: Noncollapsibility is not identical to confounding — some measures (OR, HR) are noncollapsible even without confounding. Greenland (2021): distinguishing the two prevents spurious "paradox" diagnoses.
open_question: Which effect measures (RR, OR, RD) are collapsible under what conditions — an active debate in biostatistics

name: Historical Statistical Origins
core_concern: Documenting that aggregate and partial associations can differ or reverse
primary_venue: Biometrika; Journal of the Royal Statistical Society
key_claim: The reversal is a well-defined mathematical property of weighted averages, not a logical paradox — formalised by Blyth (1972)
open_question: Whether "disappearing association" (Pearson/Yule) and "sign reversal" (Cohen/Nagel) are the same phenomenon or two distinct effects

name: Philosophy of Science / Probabilistic Causality
core_concern: Whether probabilistic associations alone can ground causal claims — the paradox is the stress test
primary_venue: Philosophy of Science; Nous; Cambridge studies in probability/induction
key_claim: Cartwright (1979): causes must raise probabilities relative to ALL background contexts, not just the aggregate. Statistical accounts of causation fail without this constraint.
open_question: Whether the probabilistic causality framework is ultimately reducible to a causal graph account (Pearl) or remains genuinely distinct
